old.name: H2O Extreme
old.teaser: The senior school, moved south to Galu where the water is clearest and the beach widest.
old.body: The south coast's longest-running kite school, IKO-affiliated, now at Blue Marlin on Galu — moved from mid-strip because, in its own words, the water is clearer, the beach wider, the riding better. Its wind page defines the seasons the whole beach lives by: kaskazi, mid-December to mid-March, 15–20 knots filling in around 10:30; kusi, June to mid-September, 18–22 knots, cooler and gustier. The reef-locked lagoon holds waist-deep flat water at every tide. Also rents wingfoil, windsurf, SUP, kayaks. Its site hides prices from robots — confirm rates by WhatsApp. Blue Marlin Beach Hotel, Galu · daily 09:00–18:00 · outside the two wind windows there is nothing to teach

r-kite254.note: the wind and the radio helmets; the course-and-what's-missing angle is in craft

old.name: Kite254
old.teaser: Radio helmets — the coach in your ear, out on the southern flat.
old.body: Two bases — the quiet southern Galu stretch at Pallet Cafe, and Diani Sea Lodge — teaching on current Ozone kites with radio-helmet instruction, so students hear the coach in real time on the water. Published, fair prices: 3-hour taster USD 130 semi-private / 210 private; 3-day intro USD 375 (2:1); 4-day full course USD 480–720, gear included. Downwinders and kite day-trips toward Funzi when the season allows. Pallet Cafe & Diani Sea Lodge · daily 10:00–18:00 · WhatsApp +254 719 891 835

r-crab.note: the sites and the wreck; the course angle is in craft

old.name: Diving the Crab
old.teaser: The grand old house: six instructors, Nitrox, 29 sites within forty minutes.
old.body: Taking divers out since 1985, based at the Nomad beach with its own training pool. It created the coast's signature wreck by re-sinking the MV Alpha Funguo off Diani as an artificial reef: upright at 22–30 m, deck and holds intact, barracuda and trevally schooling over the hull, morays and frogfish below — Advanced Open Water territory, run almost daily in season. October–March brings calm seas and visibility often to 30 m; June–September the kusi chops it down and the shops teach instead. At Nomad · daily 07:00–17:00 · +254 723 108 108 · whale sharks Nov–Feb per its listing

old.name: Ocean Tribe Scuba
old.teaser: The younger shop: ten sites in a half-hour ride, current-year paperwork on the site.
old.body: SSI-affiliated (crossover courses offered), based at The 41 Beach Club with a booking office at Baobab Beach Resort. Ten local sites — Tiwi Wall, Kisima Mungu, Galu, Mwanamoji, the Funguo wreck — plus full-day dhow trips to Kisite. Publishes a 2026 price-list PDF and instructor calendar: rare, checkable currency. Honest note from its own pages: its whale-shark trips are NOT running for the 2025/26 season. The 41 Beach Club · WhatsApp +254 700 934 854 · book the day before

old.group: Above & beyond — the sky and the blue water
old.name: Skydive Swahili
old.teaser: Forty seconds of freefall over the reef stripes, sand landing at Blue Marlin.
old.body: KCAA-licensed, USPA- and UPT-affiliated, jumping year-round with beach landings in front of the hotel. Tandem USD 350, media +100 (obs. 2026-08). The fact that matters for a day off: closed Tuesday and Wednesday. Its competitor Go Jump Kenya (tandem USD 399, beach ops at The 41) flew Kenya's first organised HALO loads at the March 2026 Kenya Boogie — the drop zone is genuinely alive. Blue Marlin, Galu · Thu–Mon 08:00–18:00 · WhatsApp +254 717 907 907 · dry-season mornings for the clearest colours

old.group: Above & beyond — the sky and the blue water
old.name: Diani Fishing Club
old.teaser: Three named boats to the Pemba Channel drop-offs — a Kenya-record blue marlin in Dec 2024.
old.body: Princess Layla, Shuwari and White Dove work the Pemba Channel and Shimoni drop-offs for blue, black and striped marlin, sailfish, wahoo, dorado and tuna, under a stated tag-and-release policy for billfish. The feed showed tournaments through March 2025 and news of a Kenya-record 785 lb blue marlin in December 2024. Peak October–April on the north-flowing currents; a July day off should not expect sailfish. The site masks its phone — book by form. Diani central · charters depart early morning · book well ahead Dec–Feb

old.group: Above & beyond — the sky and the blue water
old.name: Whale Shark Adventures
old.teaser: Two hours with a hydrophone over the side — whale song through the hull.
old.body: Run by the founder of the East African Whale Shark Trust: humpback-watching when the Antarctic migration passes (whales from early July, peak early August to mid-October) on two-hour trips with a hydrophone, EUR 75; spotter-plane whale-shark expeditions in the windows the operator gives as Feb–Mar and mid-Aug–Dec. The honesty the whole strip needs: operators' whale-shark season claims conflict (Nov–Feb, Oct–Mar, Feb–Mar), sightings are genuinely hit-and-miss, and nobody selling a guarantee is telling the truth. Sold as a search, it is a fine one. Diani central · WhatsApp +254 720 555 222 · sea-state dependent, always

old.name: The ship with no nails
old.teaser: Two thousand years of the sewn mtepe — planks stitched with coconut cord, not one iron fastening.
old.body: The oldest sailing directions for this coast — the Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea , first century AD — describe 'sewed boats' at the market-town of Rhapta, named from the Greek for sewing. Fourteen centuries later Vasco da Gama's own chronicler logged the same ship, verbatim: 'There are no nails, and the planks are held together by cords... The sails are made of palm-matting.' That was the mtepe: pegged and sewn with coir rolled from coconut husk, and it survived so late that James Hornell wrote its obituary in the Mariner's Mirror in 1941. The last sewn hulls faded out between the 1920s and 1940s; about six models and a dozen photographs are all that remain. ★ The old hand's point: sewing is not primitive nailing — stitches clamp the planks at hundreds of points and let the hull flex, so a sewn ship survives the drying coral landings that spring a nailed hull's fastenings. And note what the 1498 chronicler saw beside the cordage: 'Genoese needles, quadrants, and navigating charts' — the no-nails ship was sailed by fully instrumented navigators. Touch it today: the mtepe models in the Fort Jesus museum, Mombasa — a day trip from Diani since the bypass

old.name: How the jahazi killed the mtepe
old.teaser: The nailed dhow won — and two of its children still sail from Shimoni with names.
old.body: The nailed jahazi — Persian jahāz , ship — ended the sewn mtepe's two thousand years, and a 2023 study of Lamu's boatbuilding village Matondoni records the succession the way a shipwright would: the two coexisted until the trade 'needed a stronger vessel' — heavier cargoes, harder driving, iron fastenings. The ocean trade itself died within living memory: Marion Kaplan rode the last of it in 1974 for National Geographic — the piece was titled 'Twilight of the Arab Dhow' — as diesel and containers finished what sail had carried for a millennium. But the hulls changed cargo instead of dying: the biggest sailing dhow on the Kisite run, Monsoon , was built at Shimoni by Shirazi shipwrights, and sails for Pilli Pipa beside Almasi (launched 2014); the dhow Waswila works the same water, and in Mombasa the ex-cargo jahazi Nawalilkher now carries dinner instead of mangrove poles. ★ The old hand's point: a wooden working boat survives by changing cargo, not by changing itself — that is why boatbuilding skills still get paid at Shimoni. And Matondoni's launch ritual, 'trying the sail' before the whole village, is acceptance testing as social contract. Touch it today: board Monsoon or Almasi at Shimoni on the dhow day — the full brief is in this guide's dhow section

old.name: The ngalawa's outriggers
old.teaser: The canoe on your beach carries a rig idea that crossed from Indonesia via Madagascar.
old.body: The little double-outrigger working the Diani–Chale lagoon carries the most far-fetched pedigree of any boat on this sand. The classic case, laid out by the fisheries ethnographer James Hornell in 1919: the double outrigger is Austronesian technology, at home from Indonesia to the Pacific, reaching East Africa with the same seaborne movement that made Madagascar a Malagasy-speaking island. Modern scholarship supports the Madagascar link; the exact route and date are still argued — A.H.J. Prins titled his 1959 paper on the subject 'Uncertainties in Coastal Cultural History', and the argument has now outlived a century. ★ The old hand's point: an outrigger is a lever, not a keel — the windward float flies, the leeward float skims, and a hull too narrow to stand up to a sail becomes a stable platform drawing centimetres. Exactly what a fringing-reef coast demands. The deeper lesson: this ocean was a highway, not a barrier. Touch it today: first light off Diani or Galu — ask a fisher to show you the pito lashings; still cordage, not bolts

old.name: Wearing round
old.teaser: Why a dhow turns her stern through the wind — and what the manoeuvre says about a whole ocean.
old.body: The rig you see on the Wasini channel is technically a settee — a lateen with the front corner cut off, a form already carved on a second-century gravestone. Its price is paid at every change of board: the sail sits to the side of the mast, so on one tack the mast presses into the canvas — the documented 'bad tack'. To tack properly the crew must peak the long yard vertical and carry it bodily around the mast; which is why dhow crews prefer to wear round, turning the stern through the wind, where the wind helps swing the yard instead of fighting it. ★ The old hand's point: watch a dhow put about and you are watching risk management — wearing gives up ground to leeward but keeps that enormous yard under control. You can read the whole culture from the one manoeuvre: long offshore legs, harbours chosen so you rarely beat, and passages timed to a fair monsoon so the boat almost never fights the wind at all. Touch it today: from the bow of a Shimoni dhow, watch the channel traffic change board

old.name: The Pilot of Malindi
old.teaser: Did the great Ahmad ibn Majid really pilot da Gama? The scholars say no — and the truth is better.
old.body: Ahmad ibn Majid, born at Julfar around the 1430s, was the greatest of the Indian Ocean's mu'allims — master navigators — author of the Kitab al-Fawa'id , an encyclopedia of the whole ocean: star rhumbs, monsoon timings, port latitudes. The legend says he took Vasco da Gama from Malindi to Calicut in 1498. The record says: da Gama was turned away at Mombasa, welcomed at Malindi, and sailed on 24 April with a pilot the sultan supplied — 23 days of open water on the first of the southwest monsoon. The ibn Majid identification rests on a Meccan chronicle written eighty years later (which adds that he was drunk); modern scholarship rejects it — the eyewitness accounts call the pilot a Gujarati, and ibn Majid was by then near seventy and writing of his seafaring as done. The proof of what the pilot knew came on the return: da Gama left India against the calendar, took over ninety days to re-cross, and lost roughly half his crews to scurvy — burning the São Rafael off this coast for want of men. ★ The old hand's point: on this ocean the departure date was the navigation — 23 days with the monsoon, 90-plus and half the companies dead against it. Whoever stood on that quarterdeck, the point stands: the Portuguese did not discover this route; they were handed it. Touch it today: the seaward ramparts of Fort Jesus overlook the harbour mouth where da Gama's fleet was turned away, a century before the fort existed

old.name: Stars to find the coast, marks to live through it
old.teaser: Latitude by finger-widths, then Wasini's peaks 'their own breadth open of Rashid point'.
old.body: Offshore, the dhow navigator's latitude tool was the kamal — a small wooden card on a knotted string, one end gripped in the teeth, altitude counted in isba', finger-widths of about 1°36'; tie a knot for the latitude of a known port and the passage becomes 'sail until your knot fits, then run down the latitude.' At Wasini's latitude Polaris sits below the horizon, so the work ran on substitute stars from ibn Majid's tables. But stars only find the coast — they do not thread a live reef. For that the isharat tradition took over, codified in the 1889 Africa Pilot : make the land on the Wasini peaks, 'visible as far as from Pemba island', then bring them 'their own breadth open of Rashid point' to clear the outlying reef — past two islets 'each about 30 feet in length' whose Swahili names, Kisite and Mpunguti, are unchanged on today's chart. ★ The old hand's point: two navigations stitched together — celestial latitude to hit the coast, transit marks to thread it, because steep-to coral gives the sounding lead no warning. That is still this reef's truth: GPS tells you where you are, not where the break is. Whoever cons a tender into Chale's lagoon today does it the 1889 way — by water colour and marks in line. Touch it today: on the dhow out of Shimoni, watch the captain take the reef by eye — past the very islets the Pilot names

old.name: One round trip a year
old.teaser: Kaskazi out, kusi home — and the wintering-over that made the Swahili world.
old.body: The 1889 Admiralty Africa Pilot sets the calendar precisely: the northeast monsoon reaches this coast in mid-to-late November through a fortnight of calms and squalls; the southwest arrives around March and blows full force June to September. A nahodha who ran down from the Gulf in December could not sail home until the kusi set in — months in port, selling dates and salt fish, loading ivory and boriti mangrove poles cut in bays like Gazi for the treeless Gulf, taking wives. The wintering-over is the intermarriage, and the Swahili language and towns are its sediment. The physics enforced it: the Pilot logs the coastal current off this reef at one knot with you in kaskazi and three knots against you in kusi — and notes the inshore channel behind Wasini was worth taking precisely because 'all current is thereby avoided.' ★ The old hand's point: the monsoon was a calendar, not a forecast — one round trip a year, and the port stay was the business model, not dead time. Kenya's south coast towns exist because captains had to stay. Touch it today: Gazi's mangroves supplied the boriti trade — the community boardwalk stands in the cutting grounds; the ngalawa off Galu still sail the same seasonal wind

old.name: One night in Mombasa, 1331
old.teaser: The first eyewitness of this coast found island cities that trusted the monsoon with their bread.
old.body: Coming down from Mogadishu on a monsoon ship in 1331, Ibn Battuta left the earliest surviving eyewitness account of Mombasa: an island with fruit trees but no cereals, its grain imported by sea, its people living 'chiefly of bananas and fish', 'pious, honourable, and upright', their wooden mosques well-built. He stayed one night and sailed for Kilwa — 'very fine and substantially built'. One wrinkle scholars still chew: he calls Kilwa's buildings wood, yet the excavated Kilwa of exactly that period is coral stone. Either way the portrait stands: a string of rich, Muslim island cities provisioned entirely by dhow, fully networked into the Indian Ocean a century and a half before the Portuguese. ★ The old hand's point: an island city that imports its grain trusts the monsoon absolutely — Mombasa's food security in 1331 was a shipping schedule. And the port lunch was bananas and fish because that is what an island with fruit trees and a reef produces; provisioning-by-sea is the oldest local trade a visiting galley joins. Touch it today: Mombasa Old Town sits on the town he slept in; Diani's own Kongo Mosque is the south coast's surviving piece of that mosque-building shore

old.name: One galleot against a coast
old.teaser: Mir Ali Beg flipped the whole coast with 80 men — and Fort Jesus is the receipt.
old.body: In 1585–86 the Ottoman corsair Mir Ali Beg came down this coast with a single galleot and about eighty men — and sailed home having taken the allegiance of every major Swahili port but Malindi, three laden Portuguese ships, a gathered fleet of some 24 vessels and roughly 150,000 cruzados. He returned in 1588–89 with five galleots; Goa had learned, and Tomé de Sousa Coutinho sealed Mombasa harbour with eighteen ships and burned the Turkish flotilla. Then the land intervened: the Portuguese chronicles say thousands of the Zimba — a people the chroniclers called cannibals — fell on Mombasa from the mainland, and Ali Beg's men were destroyed between them and the guns. Historians treat the Zimba narrative and its numbers with open scepticism; the dispute is part of the record. What is not disputed is the consequence: shaken by how cheaply one corsair had flipped a coastline, Portugal built Fort Jesus in 1593–96. ★ The old hand's point: on a monsoon coast, sea power is timing plus legitimacy, not tonnage — one galleot with the right wind and the right offer detached a coast from an empire. And read chronicles like log books kept by an interested party: the numbers in a victor's account are weapons too. Touch it today: Fort Jesus is the corsair's monument — built expressly against the Ottomans after these raids

old.name: Thirty-three months
old.teaser: The siege that ended Portuguese Mombasa was decided at sea — by seven days.
old.body: On 13 March 1696 the fleet of Saif bin Sultan, Imam of Oman, shut between fifty and seventy Portuguese soldiers and several hundred African and Swahili defenders inside Fort Jesus. The siege ran almost 33 months and was decided on the water: Queen Fatuma of Zanzibar sent three dhows of supplies — captured and burned; relief squadrons from Goa broke through three times, but plague and hunger did the rest. By December 1698 the garrison was the captain, nine men and a priest. The fort fell on 13 December; a Portuguese relief fleet raised Mombasa on the 20th — seven days too late, after nearly three years. Two centuries of Portuguese power on this coast ended by a week's sailing. ★ The old hand's point: a fortress on an island is a ship at permanent anchor — it lives exactly as long as its sea lifeline. The monsoon meant relief could only sail in narrow windows; the Omanis needed only to hold the blockade between them. Blockade, not bombardment, took Fort Jesus. Touch it today: walk the seaward rampart — the gun line that watched the relief fleet arrive a week late

old.name: The Santo António de Tanná
old.teaser: The relief frigate that died with the fort — and what her guns confess about an empire.
old.body: Sent from Goa with the relief effort, the frigate Santo António de Tanná was lost under Fort Jesus's walls in 1697, the year before the fort fell. Nearly three centuries later the Institute of Nautical Archaeology and the National Museums of Kenya excavated her over three seasons (1977–80), diving thousands of hours from a barge moored in the working harbour — one of the pioneering scientific underwater excavations in sub-Saharan Africa. Her cargo held the whole Indian Ocean: African and Indian pottery, Chinese porcelain, the crew's everyday gear. And one finding cuts deep: her recovered ordnance was lighter and more limited than a ship of her size and purpose should have carried. ★ The old hand's point: a ship tied to a doomed fortress shares its fate — she had no sea room, and sea room is a ship's life. And you can read an empire's exhaustion in an armament inventory: by 1697 Portugal was garrisoning the rim of an ocean on credit. Touch it today: her pottery, porcelain and two bronze cannons are displayed in the Fort Jesus museum, metres from where she lies

old.name: The dhow chasers
old.teaser: Open boats against the slave trade in exactly the water your dhow day crosses.
old.body: From 1874 the Royal Navy kept HMS London, an old two-decker turned depot ship, moored at Zanzibar to suppress the Indian Ocean slave trade — and the real work fell to her small boats: 39 slave dhows taken in these channels in eighteen months of 1874–76. The cost showed on 3 December 1881, when Captain Charles Brownrigg boarded a dhow carrying around a hundred enslaved people between Pemba and Zanzibar and was cut down at the gunwale with part of his crew; Lieutenant Lloyd Mathews hunted the slaver to Wete and took him, mortally wounded. The honest first-hand account is G.L. Sulivan's Dhow Chasing in Zanzibar Waters (1873) — five years of it, frank about how often the trade slipped through. ★ The old hand's point: the fighting unit was never the big ship — it was an open boat and a boarding over a low gunwale where rank protected nobody; a post-captain died exactly as an able seaman would. And the arithmetic is honest: 39 dhows in a trade of thousands — patrols raised the price of slaving; treaties and the 1873 closure of Zanzibar's market did the rest. These channels rewarded shallow draft, local knowledge and the land breeze, and the dhow skippers held all three. Touch it today: the patrol ground is the water between Shimoni and the Kisite reefs; ashore, the Shimoni caves hold the trade's shore story

old.name: Bamvua and msindizo
old.teaser: The Diani–Chale fishery runs on the moon twice over — and the month is opened by radio from Zanzibar.
old.body: Researchers who censused every landing from Diani to Gazi in 2003–06 wrote down the calendar the fishers actually keep. The lunar month opens with the first sighting of the waxing crescent — coordinated, remarkably, by daily radio broadcast from Zanzibar — and the spring tides bracketing new and full moon are bamvua , the prime fishing days; neaps are msindizo , 'to rest', when trap fishers stay ashore rather than set gear in the dark of a late low. The fishers even corrected the scientists' grid: Diani's lagoon is shallower than Chale's, so the same afternoon can be resting water at Chale and bamvua at Mwaepe. Over a year the clock adds to roughly 570 fishers, 85,551 fisher-days and about 403 tonnes of fish. ★ The old hand's point: the moon makes the tide and the sighted crescent makes the month, so religion and hydrography agree on which mornings a canoe goes out. Ask any captain ' bamvua au msindizo? ' — the question marks you as someone who understands this sea, and it tells a chef exactly which dawns the auction is worth walking to. Touch it today: any landing at first light — on a bamvua day the beach crowds with ngalawa; on msindizo it is nearly empty

old.name: Kuchukua — the women's fishery
old.teaser: The women of the flats do not call themselves fishers — and land half of what this coast eats at home.
old.body: A 2021–23 survey of 141 fishers in the Shimoni–Vanga seascape mapped a sea divided by gender: men beyond the reef crest with handlines and basket traps; women on the seagrass flats on foot — hand-gathering, and hunting octopus with a pointed stick. The women call the work kuchukua , 'to take', and pointedly do not call themselves wavuvi — fishers — while every man interviewed did. Their calendar is the tide's: octopus only in the bamvua windows, eight days twice a month, when the flats dry enough to walk. They average 3.5 hours at sea, nine days a month, against the men's five hours on twenty-one — and their catch supplies about half of all seafood eaten at home. Girls have their own technique, kuranda, sweeping small fish into a held cloth; ashore the mama chemsha boil and hawk the sardine catch. ★ The old hand's point: half the protein of this coast is caught by people who insist they are not fishers, on legs instead of hulls, in a fishery timed entirely by spring tides. The reef flat is a tidal larder with an eight-day combination lock. Touch it today: at spring low from Diani to Wasini, the lines of women crossing the flats with buckets and sticks are the fishery working

old.name: Munje's octopus gamble
old.teaser: The village that caught more by not fishing — 650 kg in three days off a rested flat.
old.body: At Munje, between Diani and Msambweni, the Beach Management Unit closed a 4,000 m² patch of reef flat to octopus fishing in mid-2023. Fishers Salim Juma Shee and Kassim Ali Siwa opposed it — Shee later became one of its monitors. When the reef reopened for three days that October, timed to the low, the village landed about 650 kg of octopus; one fisher took over thirty kilos in a morning where two had been normal. The proceeds run on a strict published split between welfare, the BMU and the active fishers, and the supporting NGO is frank that its first closure failed for lack of sensitisation. The elders' baseline is the argument: in their fathers' days there was a lot of octopus here. ★ The old hand's point: octopus fishing is spring-tide work whether you legislate or not — what Munje added is the fallow. Treat a reef flat like a field: rest it three to four months, harvest on the big low. Restraint here is a gear type, and it out-fishes the daily speargun. Touch it today: opening days (every 3–4 months) are village events — the single best moment on this coast to buy pweza, hours old by the hundredweight

old.name: The landings that said no
old.teaser: Two Diani beaches kept the pull seines off by tradition alone — and out-fished the neighbours.
old.body: A 1997 study of the Diani–Chale area recorded one of the oldest and most elaborate traditions of sacred sea-sites on the Kenyan coast — spirit places fishers hesitated even to name, offerings at annual ceremonies, a sea populated by the playful kibwengo and the drowning kitunusi. The customs were never fisheries management — their purpose, the paper is careful to say, was to appease spirits, not regulate stocks. And yet two Diani landings, Mvuleni and Mwanyaza , kept the destructive pull seines off their beaches for more than twenty years by argument from tradition alone, while neighbouring landings adopted the gear — and the measurements came out on the elders' side, with higher per-capita catches at the two refusing beaches. ★ The old hand's point: this is the truest lesson in the whole Diani story — customary authority measurably protected livelihoods even though conservation was never its purpose. A sailor recognises the mechanism at once: port discipline, enforced by respect rather than regulation, working exactly as far as respect reached. Today's Beach Management Units are its legal descendants. Touch it today: Mvuleni and Mwanyaza are still working landing beaches, a short walk from the hotels — buy your fish there and you stand in the story

x-crab-course.note: the course: open enrolment, named instructors; the sites are in the sea fold

old.name: ★ Diving the Crab
old.teaser: A PADI 5★ IDC resort: the tier that certifies instructors, not just divers.
old.body: Why this one. The coast's senior dive operation has worked this reef since 1985, and it is a PADI 5 Star IDC Resort — the level that trains new instructors, not merely new divers. That means you can start here never having breathed underwater and, if you keep coming back, end up qualified to teach it, on the same reef the whole way. Own pool, Nitrox, six instructors, around twenty-nine sites within a forty-minute boat ride. And it has been here long enough to change the seabed: it created the coast's signature wreck by re-sinking the MV Alpha Funguo as an artificial reef. Based at the Nomad beach · book the course, not a single dive, if you want the ladder divingthecrab.com →

old.group: The others, and what each is missing
old.name: Kite254
old.teaser: Radio-helmet coaching in a waist-deep lagoon — you hear the fix mid-mistake.
old.body: Two bases , current Ozone kites, and radio-helmet instruction so the coaching arrives while you are still making the error rather than afterwards on the beach. The waist-deep, reef-protected lagoon is the pedagogy: you can stand up and start again. Roughly six months of trade wind a year. Missing: same as above — no named instructor published. Bases at Pallet Cafe on southern Galu and at Diani Sea Lodge kite254.com →

old.group: The others, and what each is missing
old.name: H2O Extreme
old.teaser: Kiting here since 2003, IKO-certified — and it moved beach to teach on better water.
old.body: Two decades on this water and IKO-affiliated, so the certificate is a real one. It moved from central Diani to Galu for a reason it states plainly: clearer water, wider beach, better riding away from the mid-strip tides and boat traffic. A school that relocates to improve its teaching water is taking the teaching seriously. Missing: no instructor is named publicly — a reputable room, but you do not know whose hands you are in until you arrive. Its wind page defines the two seasons properly — kaskazi N/NE mid-Dec to mid-March, kusi the rest h2o-extreme.com →

x-akamba.group: The others, and what each is missing
x-akamba.note: one home for Akamba: the carving, buying at source, what is missing

old.group: The others, and what each is missing
old.name: Akamba Handicraft Co-operative
old.teaser: Since 1963, ~2,800 carvers, and 70–80% of each sale goes to the maker.
old.body: Founded in 1963 by around a hundred Kamba carvers who brought the Wamunyu tradition to Mombasa, now roughly 2,800 members working rosewood, ebony and neem by hand. You walk the open sheds and watch a piece go from log selection through rough carving, detailing and finishing — and buy from the co-op store, where seventy to eighty per cent goes to the carver , against a fraction of that on the beach. Missing: no classes. You can watch and buy, and you can meet the individual carvers, but you cannot join. Buy here rather than on the sand — and see the warning below on what “ebony” usually is akambahandicraftcoop.com →

old.group: The cloth & the carving — buy at source
old.name: Akamba Handicraft Co-operative
old.teaser: 2,800 carvers, axe and chisel, no machines — where the beach-stall carvings actually come from.
old.body: Founded by about 100 Kamba carvers who brought the Wamunyu tradition to Mombasa; today roughly 2,800 members work rosewood, ebony and neem in open sheds you can walk, and the co-op store returns 70–80% of each sale to the maker. The honest test for 'ebony' anywhere on this coast: weight and end-grain — real mpingo is heavy and dark to the core; the shoe-polished fakes are neither. Pair with an airport run: industrial Changamwe, 45–60 ferry-free minutes from Diani since the bypass. Off Port Reitz Road, Changamwe · +254 746 233 118 · weekday mornings, sheds fullest

old.name: Diani Art Club
old.tag: missing: it's a gallery, not a school
old.teaser: Jimmy, the resident portrait painter — the one named practising maker on this list.
old.body: A working gallery on the Ukunda–Diani road dedicated to Kenyan artists, from bold abstracts to Maasai handcraft, with resident portrait painter Jimmy taking commissions — and real, seasonally published opening hours, which on this strip is itself a mark of seriousness. Missing: commissions, not classes. If you want something made by a named person you can meet, this is it; if you want to learn to make it, this is not. It also sells safari bookings, which tells you its scale honestly diani-artclub.com →

old.name: Diani Art Club
old.teaser: The strip's one working gallery — Kenyan painters, a resident portraitist, real published hours.
old.body: Small, commercial and honest about it: Kenyan artists on the walls, portrait commissions by WhatsApp from resident painter Jimmy, safari bookings on the side. Opposite the GPS petrol station on the Ukunda–Diani road — not on the map apps, which tells you the scale. Go for the painting wall. Ukunda–Diani road · +254 703 648 892 · Sundays only in high season (Sep–Feb)

old.name: The Kaaribu street-food walk
old.teaser: A registered company, a fixed route, and the door into rooms you would not enter alone.
old.body: Ninety minutes with Kaaribu Experiences, a registered Kenyan company: meet at Tsunami Garden Cafe, walk the Ibiza market trading cluster, eat in a kibandaski — cardamom-coconut porridge, viazi karai, chapati and beans, ugali na sukuma, coconut rice with fish — and finish with an mnazi tasting. It is the honest way into the mangwe , which is not a walk-in. Bookable as an outsider · the market and the palm-wine dens both come with it kaaribu.com →

old.name: What is sold as craft and is not
old.teaser: Most of the “ebony” on this beach is lighter wood under shoe polish.
old.body: Real mpingo is heavy and dark all the way through; scratch an unseen face and see whether the colour survives. Most stall “ebony” on the strip does not. Buy at the Akamba co-op sheds instead, where the carver keeps seventy to eighty per cent, and expect to pay more for a piece that is what it says it is. The same applies to the story: do not believe a line about a grandfather unless you are watching the grandfather. Bargaining is expected on the beach; it is not expected at the co-op or from a named artist

old.name: Biashara Street, Mombasa
old.teaser: The kanga street: five generations of fabric houses, tailors hemming while you wait.
old.body: The kikois and kangas on Diani's stalls are near-universally factory prints bought wholesale here. Mali ya Abdulla — the Kaderdina Hajee Essak house, founded 1887, on this street since 1907 — is so established that leso patterns carry its name. Kangas sell in pairs (a doti), each printed with a proverb, the jina: have a Swahili speaker translate before you gift one — the proverbs have teeth. Combine with Old Town; quieter Friday midday. Mwembe Tayari end of Mombasa CBD · bargaining standard, respectfully

old.name: Kentaste, Ukunda
old.teaser: The coconut cream on every Kenyan shelf is pressed minutes from the beach.
old.body: Founded 2014 as a Kwale family business: cream, milk, virgin oil, desiccated, flour and chips from over 4,000 smallholders across the coast counties, roughly half certified organic/Fairtrade, exported to three continents. No tours — a working plant — but the galley consequence is real: the local, traceable pantry coconut sits on the Carrefour and Chandarana shelves at source prices. Stock it instead of flying tins in. Ukunda outskirts · buy the products on the strip

old.name: Kenya Bixa, Tiwi
old.teaser: The annatto that colours the world's cheddar is processed on the Diani side of Kwale.
old.body: Quiet terroir fact: the orange annatto (achiote) in smoked fish, rubs and half the world's cheese is processed at Tiwi — 1,000–1,400 tonnes of bixa seed a year from 7,000–10,000 contracted smallholders, farm-gate KES 95/kg (obs. 2026-08), with a government drive launched in August 2026 to double production. The spiky red bixa pods grow along south-coast smallholdings; a chef who knows achiote will start seeing the hedges everywhere. Include it as story — there are no tours and no factory shop; buy achiote seed at the spice stalls instead. Tiwi · an export works, not an attraction
